entry.title: Dilemma Dynamics: decision quality and the dynamics of cooperation

link.title: Dilemma Dynamics: decision quality and the dynamics of cooperation

entry.content:
Exploring AI strategies, incentives and cooperation.

Recognising a profitable action and sustaining a cooperative relationship are distinct capabilities. Dilemma Dynamics makes that distinction visible in 7,104 repeated-game episodes with NVIDIA Nemotron Nano and Super. A short private draft reduced average benchmark decision loss by 16.8–37.5% across two models and two temperatures. The same procedure increased loss against Tit-for-Tat and produced less cooperation in autonomous self-play.

Play & understand → Explore the results →

A game where another encounter matters

In the repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma, both players choose privately and reveal together. Mutual cooperation earns three points each; mutual defection earns one each. Defecting against a cooperator earns five, leaving the cooperator zero. Defection pays more immediately, but a responsive partner can make cooperation valuable over time. Each player seeks their own cumulative points.

The evaluation compares two procedures. Direct makes one thinking-off action request. Draft generates a thinking-on draft of up to 1,024 tokens, then makes a separate thinking-off action request of up to 128 tokens using that draft. Both run at temperatures 0 and 1, with matched schedules and top-p 1. The comparison measures this complete two-stage procedure.

The 6,144 benchmark episodes use four disclosed opponent rules: Always Cooperate, Always Defect, Tit-for-Tat and Grim. Exact dynamic programming finds the best achievable expected own payoff for each choice. Decision loss is the normalised payoff forgone by an action, allowing optimal play afterward. A reduction in loss means fewer points given up; it is separate from a percentage gain in earned reward.

Drafting improves the average

The effect depends on the partner. Against Always Cooperate, better own-payoff decisions mean exploiting an unresponsive cooperator. Against Grim, today’s defection can destroy future gains. Against Tit-for-Tat, the optimal pattern changes with the chance of another round: some conditions reward alternation, others sustained cooperation.

Tit-for-Tat reverses the average finding in all four model/temperature comparisons. Draft raises its mean decision loss by 0.1717–0.3225 normalised payoff points, while lowering all four means against Always Cooperate and Grim. The condition chart shows why the opponent response and horizon belong in the explanation of a model’s score.

Cooperation also depends on repair

Another 960 autonomous dyads cover all ten model/procedure pairings, including self-play. Each pairing has 48 episodes per temperature. Changing both self-play agents from Direct to Draft lowers mutual-cooperation and joint-return point estimates for each model at each temperature.

Super at temperature zero illustrates the role of recovery. Direct self-play starts with no mutually cooperative first rounds, then returns to cooperation in 82 of 218 eligible transitions. Draft has no observed return to mutual cooperation in 325 opportunities. Direct accumulates 124/376 cooperative rounds, compared with 3/376 under Draft. These are round counts, with a different denominator from the episode-weighted chart. Cooperation can emerge through the history of interaction even when it is absent at the start.

What these patterns open up

The results connect three questions that are useful to study separately: Can an agent identify the best action against a known policy? Can it plan through that policy’s future responses? Can two adaptive agents establish and repair a productive relationship?

The PDF notes develop future work on explicit contingent planning, forgiving partners, communication and noisy observations, longer interactions, and more varied incentives and populations. Controlled repair opportunities could reveal when cautious play becomes a persistent low-cooperation pattern. Adding messages or noisy actions would show how agents interpret mistakes, commitments and intent. Broader games and populations would test how these capabilities transfer across changing social environments.

Evidence and methods

Matched environments interleave both temperatures across 48 blocks, balanced between action-label mappings and display seats. The four drafting comparisons were fixed before this campaign’s outcomes; opponent, self-play and presentation slices are exploratory. The released action histories reproduce exact scores, contrasts and figures offline. Native Inspect AI logs, local MLflow tracking and frozen source records connect execution to that analysis.

The comparison concerns the stated models, procedures and environments. Temperature comparisons use nominal 95% intervals, and exploratory comparisons have no family correction. Measured token use and request timing describe the resources used; usage-based cost estimates use the rates recorded during the run.

  • Read the study and mathematical notes (PDF)
  • Browse the repository and reproduction instructions

Explore the app

Start with Play & understand to learn the rules, play yourself, watch bots or watch labelled Nemotron recordings. Completed rounds include payoff analysis. Results leads with charts and key numbers, followed by optional Study replay and detailed tables. The initial recording is selected by fixed metadata, independently of its outcome.

Recreational games offers Tic-tac-toe and Dots & Boxes. They are mathematical games on discrete grids or lattices, with perfect information and visible sequential moves; their rules and tactical ideas are explained in that area.

The website supports free browser play, saved games and replay exports. Live Nemotron play is available by launching the same app locally, with a key held by the localhost server and calls explicitly started on your account.
entry.summary: A 7,104-episode Nemotron evaluation: drafting improves average payoff decisions, while opponent responses reveal a different story for reciprocity and cooperation.

entry.title: Bayesian Orchestrator
entry.content:
Since March, I have been spending pretty much all my weekends doing… homework. Why? In March, I joined the AI Performance Engineering course at Nebius Academy, which also gave me the courage to try my own ideas and participate in the Nebius AI serverless challenge (and spend more weekends on that…). So here it goes!

There is a classic three-circle Venn diagram with cheap, fast, and good, where the intersection of these 3 bubbles is impossible. But how does one choose a possible combination depending on the task at hand, and whilst not being a trillionaire? Here, I address this problem in the context of LLM routing, and my motivation comes from a recent position paper on the need for Bayes in agentic AI orchestration.

It would be unreasonable to assume that an LLM can perform principled probabilistic reasoning (e.g. see this or this), and instead of trying to make LLMs more principled (which, in my very biased case, means more Bayesian), I built an external controller that tracks how reliable each model is and routes questions accordingly. The approach defines a hierarchical Bayesian reliability model to estimate the probability that each model will answer correctly, based on everything observed so far, that is the question type, subject matter, model identity, and picks the option with the best expected utility.

The utility function used here is rather simple but still balances accuracy against cost: utility = correctness − (cost scale × call cost), where one tunes the cost scale to express one’s preferences for increased costs versus accuracy.

Before you call a model, you can only use what you know ahead of time, which model it is, what subject the question is about, and how long the question is, which gives a pre-call probability estimate and determines which model to call first. After the model responds, the orchestrator gets more signals: how self-confident the model was, how long it took, and how many tokens it used. These go into a post-call probability estimate that determines whether the answer is given or the next model is called. If the first model’s answer looks doubtful, the orchestrator checks whether calling a second model is worth it. If the expected gain from a second call clears a threshold, it makes the call, then combines the answers using a Noisy-OR rule (which roughly says that if either model supports an answer, then that counts).

I test my idea on MMLU-Pro, a multiple-choice benchmark, with three models: two ~30B models and a 120B model, namely:

  • nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B

  • Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507

  • openai/gpt-oss-120b

For the setup, I ran it as a Nebius Serverless AI Job, which was a good fit because the workload is a finite batch evaluation: the container runs on CPU, model inference happens through APIs, every completed question-model call is checkpointed to persistent storage (meaning interrupted runs can continue without repeating paid calls).

The job samples 4000 MMLU-Pro questions, calls every configured model, checkpoints completed calls to persistent storage, fits Bayesian reliability models, and writes the final report, JSON summary, and plots. The repo is available on GitHub.

The results support the idea of Bayesian adaptive policy:

The adaptive policy called a second model on about one third of the questions. Compared to always using the big model, it’s more accurate but slightly more expensive; this could be tuned with the cost scale discussed above. The oracle looks cheap because it gets to retroactively pick the cheapest correct answer. In the real world, you don’t get to do that, so here I use the oracle as an upper bound.

LLMs themselves might be subtle predictors, but combined with Bayes-inspired reasoning, we can allocate resources more efficiently, manage costs and latencies, and adapt routing decisions as evidence accumulates. Workflows (Bayesian, please) over tools!

The project has gaps to fill, yet I feel good that I was able to build it up to its current state.

entry.summary: Or conductor for an orchestra of LLMs.
